articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Yvette Tan 
- Published 8 October 2026 
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries. 
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. 
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place. 
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. 
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter. 
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports. 
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement on Thursday that "diplomacy should prevail over emotions". 
"Despite Seoul's decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to restoring a constructive dialogue - even if it takes time," he said. 
Earlier on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said in a statement it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly". 
- 
Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
- Published 11 January 2025 
- 
Thousands of North Koreans fought for Russia. A memorial hints at the death toll 
- Published 7 May 
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive". 
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. 
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. 
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. 
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. 
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. 
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. 
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. 
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. 
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. 
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. 
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. 
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

articles.title: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he would not watch it
articles.summary: The planned execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
"I'm not going to be watching it" - JD Vance on possible livestreamed execution By Nardine Saad   and   Kali Hays 
- Published 9 October 2026 
JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution. 
The US vice-president expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the December execution would go ahead as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added that "if it's through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it". 
Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but said the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it. 
Nidal Hasan killed 13 unarmed soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009 and injured another 32. His execution would be the first military firing squad execution in more than 60 years. 
The Pentagon announced its desire to execute the former US Army major by firing squad over the attack on 3 December earlier this week. 
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth then said the execution would be livestreamed for the public, as "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things". 
Trump was asked about the possibility that visuals of Hasan's execution could be used as propaganda for terrorists as he left the White House on Friday. 
Calling Hasan "totally nuts", he replied: "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him." 
The Pentagon declined to comment further when asked for more information about a decision on the livestream. 
Vance condemned Hasan's attack on the base as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11" while speaking to reporters on Friday. 
Asked about how his Catholic faith affected his stance on the plan to stream a public execution, Vance questioned whether it would happen. 
But he noted that Hasan, a military psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems, but had instead "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived". 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Trump says he approved the livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter 
The possible livestreaming of the execution has been met with criticism from both political parties. 
Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched, warning that public executions eroded civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment". 
Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider. 
"The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent." 
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group. 
Georgia lawmaker Austin Scott, a Republican, said that while he "absolutely" supported the death sentence, livestreaming executions was "what jihadists do - America is better than that". 
John Bolton, a former national security adviser during the first Trump administration, told BBC's Radio 4 PM that he supported capital punishment, but that the livestream was "unnecessary" because there were provisions for interested parties to view the execution in person. 
"I just think this is a mark by Secretary Hegseth doing something he thinks will please President Trump," he said. "I think that's really not appropriate for a secretary of defence." 
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow". 
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture". 
Figure caption, 
Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed? 
Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines on 5 November 2009. 
He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. 
It was the deadliest ever non-combat attack on a US military base. 
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. 
When Hegseth told reporters on Thursday about his livestreaming plans, he did not specify where or how the execution would be shown. 
A Pentagon spokesperson later reiterated to the BBC that Hasan's execution "will be livestreamed" but said the government had no further details. 
The White House did not respond to an inquiry about whether it expected to show Hasan's planned execution on its social media channels. 
-

- Published 1 day ago 
-

- Published 1 day ago 
All of the social media platforms the US government has accounts on have prohibitions in place on violent images and videos, as well as those that show death or glorify or make a spectacle of violence. 
Meta - owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads - explicitly bans any livestream of capital punishment. 
YouTube bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers", while TikTok similarly bars "extremely graphic, violent or disturbing content" that includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual". 
But both YouTube and TikTok make exceptions in instances of "public interest". 
Asked whether a livestream of an execution qualifies for the exception if it is government-sanctioned, a TikTok spokeswoman said: "Regardless, I'd point you back to the not allowed section which reflects our approach." 
The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since billionaire Elon Musk took over the platform, prohibits content "glorifying" violence. 
Meta, YouTube and X did not respond to multiple BBC requests for comment.

articles.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago -  why are they resuming now?
articles.summary: The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey Bethea By Sheila Flynn Senior US reporter 
- Published 10 October 2026 
They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow. 
It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to spectators. 
By the execution time of 05:00, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000. 
That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70. 
The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream. 
Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner". The local sheriff had died four months earlier and his widow had become his unlikely replacement. 
She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was a hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death. 
That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in the US. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later. 
By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now. 
Image source, FPG/Staff/Getty Image caption, 
Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the US 
A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan , who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas. 
The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be livestreamed. 
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. 
University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked. 
"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC. 
He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining - it was at 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%. 
"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said. 
It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in. 
With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment... bring your popcorn, invite your friends". 
Figure caption, 
Americans discuss their views on the death penalty after the botched execution in Tennessee of convicted murderer Christa Pike 
Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream. 
"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up... to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific." 
Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's death in 2002, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap. 
The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution. 
"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. 
"Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific." 
But the polarisation and rhetoric in US politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University. 
"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. 
"So it's not like they're cheering a public execution - they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'" 
Figure caption, 
Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed? 
Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong. 
Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said surveys point to a declining appetite for violence in the US. 
"This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people." 
"I think it's this: a public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country." 
The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday. 
US Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned and said he would not watch it if it were livestreamed. 
Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it. 
He did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution. 
"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

articles.title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
articles.summary: Students taking to the streets have become a focal point in the country's increasingly polarised politics.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last month By Nick Beake Europe correspondent 
- Published 10 October 2026 
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets. 
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school. 
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen." 
He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds. 
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down. 
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population." 
The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis. 
Image caption, 
Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in Lille 
The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country. 
Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter. 
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protesting 
The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them. 
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million. 
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them. 
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem. 
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages. 
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils). 
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains. 
Image caption, 
Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for change 
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days. 
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget. 
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country. 
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest. 
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future." 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Police have been accused of heavy-handed tactics 
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries. 
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry. 
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks. 
But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers. 
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens. 
Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade. 
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth. 
"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether." 
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests. 
Image caption, 
Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protests 
But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests. 
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world." 
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard. 
Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring. 
"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better." 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schools 
The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise. 
More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country. 
But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape. 
The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant. 
Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration. 
Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race. 
Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon. 
Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrations 
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks. 
Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth. 
He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history. 
Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration. 
"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march. 
Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros. 
She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs. 
The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social history 
The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix. 
This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago. 
Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve. 
And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically. 
What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess. 
The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase. 
Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace. 
She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils. 
For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Many students have said they will not back down from protesting 
But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition. 
"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris. 
"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit." 
As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped. 
But not for long. 
A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street. 
"The canteen is still open." 
The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.

China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal 
Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs 
The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry. 
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers. 
The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday. “It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place. 
China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs. 
Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles. 
He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that. 
“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said. 
“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart. 
Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition. 
Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared. 
As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU. skip past newsletter promotion

China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe. 
The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday. 
A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”. 
It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”. 
While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

Mao’s Last Dancer Li Cunxin on his long-awaited follow-up: ‘I don’t think my publisher expected it to take 14 years!’ 
Tim Byrne 
As The Lucky Son picks up where Cunxin’s 2003 memoir left off, the renowned Chinese Australian ballet dancer reflects on sacrifices made by his wife, his years at a stockbroker, and his success leading the Queensland Ballet

S ome people live such extraordinary lives that a single autobiography simply won’t suffice. Li Cunxin has now written two. The renowned ballet dancer and former artistic director of Queensland Ballet had hoped he was finished writing his story after the phenomenal international success of his 2003 memoir, Mao’s Last Dancer. But life had other plans. 
“Actually, I had signed a contract with Penguin Random House for a follow-up,” Cunxin says, from his home in Brisbane. “It was going to be about the lives of my brothers and friends in China, and the ways the country has changed over time. But then I was offered the job at Queensland Ballet and I had to dedicate all my time to that. I don’t think they were expecting [the sequel] to take 14 years!” 
His second memoir, The Lucky Son, takes up precisely where Mao’s Last Dancer left off: as Cunxin and his ballet dancer wife Mary fly to their new lives at Houston Ballet under the directorship of Ben Stevenson. That outline of the proposed book on China can be glimpsed under the surface of this one, like a palimpsest; Cunxin’s six brothers’ lives are sketched, and a fascinating portrait of a country lifting itself from abject poverty to world superpower emerges. 
View image in fullscreen 
Li Cunxin and Mary McKendry in Ben Stevenson’s Sleeping Beauty in 1988. Photograph: Houston Ballet 
“One of the things my mother taught me was to keep moving forward at all times,” Cunxin says. “Don’t think about the past, just concentrate on what is ahead.” That grit kept her children alive and was instrumental in shaping Cunxin’s dogged, highly ambitious personality. 
Determination runs in the family. Mary was a deeply respected dancer herself, a career she sacrificed when she and Cunxin discovered their daughter Sophie was born profoundly deaf. “We were so fearful that Sophie would miss out on so much,” Cunxin says. “Music and dance and all the magical things.” 
Mary immediately left the world of ballet (she would return years later as ballet mistress at Queensland Ballet) to teach Sophie to talk. “Mary was incredible,” Cunxin recalls. “She gave everything to the task.” 
One one hand, it was a complete success. Sophie was fitted with a bionic ear (then known as a cochlear implant) and thrived; she embraced dance, had a successful education and excelled in the workplace. Cunxin and Mary assumed they’d done all that was needed. 
View image in fullscreen 
‘To be a leader of any kind takes vision. I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet.’ Photograph: David Kelly/The Guardian 
But then in 2015, Sophie sent an email to her parents that shocked and devastated them. Sophie expressed frustration at her parents for wanting their daughter to hear; she felt she’d come halfway to meet their world, but they had not met hers. They had not even bothered to learn sign language. Her “deafness was her birthright”, Cunxin writes in the book. Now, he says, Sophie “is a kind of ambassador between the hearing and deaf communities”. And he and Mary have begun learning Auslan. 
Cunxin’s dance career was so exemplary – moving from the Beijing Dance Academy to Houston Ballet, and then to principal artist at Australian Ballet – he could have been forgiven for hanging up his pointe shoes and walking into a lucrative position in a stockbroking firm. Indeed, that’s exactly what he did. An unsuccessful tilt at the artistic directorship of Australian Ballet (the role eventually went to David McAllister) utterly crushed him, and it seemed for a few years he would never return to the world of professional ballet. 
Of course, that wasn’t how it panned out: despite being burned by that failure, Cunxin reluctantly put his name in the hat when Queensland Ballet were looking for their next artistic director. That tenacity and resolve was once more poured into the theatre. 
“To be a leader of any kind takes vision,” Cunxin says. “I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet. But you also have to be a good communicator, because you need to inspire others to join in your vision.” And you need to apply yourself, which wasn’t such an issue for someone trained at Beijing Dance Academy, with its brutal rehearsal regime and exacting standards. 
One of the delights of The Lucky Son is the way it tracks some of our favourite characters from Mao’s Last Dancer, including The Bandit, Cunxin’s bestie at the Beijing Dance Academy; his gorgeous instructor Teacher Xiao; and his astonishing mum and dad, Niang and Dia. There are echoes in the events too: Stevenson’s trip to Queensland to watch his protégé mount Cinderella recalls the unforgettable moment in Mao’s Last Dancer when his parents leave China for the first time to see their son dance and the audience gives them a standing ovation. 
View image in fullscreen 
Cunxin at the Thomas Dixon Centre, home of the Queensland Ballet. Photograph: David Kelly/The Guardian 
Central to Cunxin’s success at Queensland Ballet – where he oversaw a massive improvement in standards and built a stunning new home for the company, the Thomas Dixon Centre – were the lessons he learned from his time away from ballet, when he was a stockbroker: “I learned so much from the business world – when we had to approach donors for money, I could speak their language.” Relationships with Elisabeth Murdoch and the Ian Potter Foundation came in handy, and he and Mary also contributed some money of their own. It’s now a world-class organisation. 
Looking back on his life now, Cunxin feels an overwhelming sense of “gratitude, for the opportunities I was given and the people and artists who shaped me”. The Lucky Son concludes on stage – hardly surprising, given so many of the key moments in Cunxin’s life have been there – but this time it is in Switzerland, where he was awarded ballet’s most prestigious award, the Prix de Lausanne, in 2025. After a few years of serious health issues (Mary is a cancer survivor and Cunxin has a major heart condition), the couple are increasingly happy to chill. “Our health has forced us to slow down,” he says with the emphasis on forced, as if there were no way they would slow down on purpose. “I worked very hard for two years on this book – it’s been all-consuming. So yes, I am enjoying taking things a little slower.”
Is he confident that ballet will survive the coming AI tsunami, given how hard the art form is to perfect and how much time and effort is required? “I am worried, but I do think ballet is special,” he says. “When people come to see ballet, they are blown away by the artistry, the physicality and the music. I think it’s more important than ever to connect people.”
